narrative.text: A list of abbreviations used in the HIV case definitions and staging publication.

The introduction explains that WHO revised its HIV case definitions for surveillance and harmonized them with clinical staging and immunological classification, to support scaling up antiretroviral therapy and track the HIV epidemic. It notes the revisions came from regional consultations in 2004–2005 and a consensus meeting in 2006, and that AIDS reporting alone no longer gives reliable data now that treatment delays AIDS.

Traces the history of WHO's AIDS case definitions from the 1985 Bangui definition through revisions in 1986, 1989 and 1994, noting weak performance of the paediatric definition. It explains that AIDS reporting in low- and middle-income countries has been incomplete, while treatment has reduced new AIDS cases and deaths where coverage is high.

Recommends that countries report newly diagnosed HIV infection in adults and children, with the same confidentiality as AIDS reporting and with providers initiating reports. It also sets the age definitions used for children, adults, youth and infants.

Sets out WHO's recommendation that new HIV cases be reported using a standard national case definition confirmed by laboratory criteria at any clinical stage. Box 1 gives the diagnostic criteria, using two antibody tests or virological tests for people aged 18 months or older and virological tests for younger children because maternal antibodies persist.

Defines advanced HIV infection, including AIDS, for reporting, based on stage 3 or 4 clinical conditions or CD4 thresholds by age. A footnote gives the stricter definition of AIDS, and the text states that separate AIDS case reporting is no longer required where HIV and advanced HIV are reported.

Describes primary HIV infection, which may be silent or cause an acute febrile illness with rash, sore throat and swollen glands a few weeks after exposure, and how it can be identified. It reviews the history of WHO clinical staging, explains that the new staging is harmonized across ages, and proposes using new or recurrent staging events to assess people on antiretroviral therapy.
A heading fragment for the section on clinical and immunological classification of HIV.

Gives the four WHO clinical stages from asymptomatic to severe and explains how staging events can guide decisions for people on antiretroviral therapy after 24 weeks, when early events may reflect immune reconstitution. It describes CD4 cell counts and percentages as the standard measure of HIV-related immune deficiency. It notes that healthy infants have much higher CD4 values than adults, which fall with age.

Table 2 gives the WHO immunological classification of HIV-associated immunodeficiency by age-specific CD4 values. Table 3 lists the clinical conditions that define stages 1 to 4 in adults and adolescents, from persistent lymphadenopathy to wasting, tuberculosis, Kaposi's sarcoma and other opportunistic infections. The block goes on to the corresponding staging for children.

An annex table giving clinical and definitive criteria for diagnosing each HIV staging event in adults and in children under 15 years. Entries range from oral ulceration, skin conditions and fungal nail infections to severe weight loss, chronic diarrhoea and oesophageal candidiasis. Stage 4 conditions such as extrapulmonary tuberculosis and visceral herpes are also covered. The end covers disseminated fungal and mycobacterial infections, which need laboratory confirmation.

Annex 2 sets out criteria for a presumptive diagnosis of severe HIV disease in HIV antibody-positive infants under 18 months, based on AIDS-indicator conditions or a combination of thrush, severe pneumonia and severe sepsis. It notes supporting factors such as maternal death or low CD4 and urges confirmation as soon as possible.
A reference list citing mainly WHO and US CDC AIDS case definitions and studies on HIV progression and staging; the extracted text ends in long runs of dots.

The title, cataloguing and copyright pages of WHO's 2007 publication on HIV case definitions for surveillance and revised clinical staging and immunological classification of HIV-related disease in adults and children, with ISBN, rights notices and contents.
